How Curriculum Standards Work

Select each card to reveal its role, how it guides lesson planning, and how it relates to classroom assessment. The descriptions below are explanatory guidance; always verify exact terminology and wording in the relevant DSKP.

1

Content Standard (CS)

The broad learning focus.

What does CS tell the teacher?

The Content Standard describes the main area of knowledge or learning focus pupils are expected to develop. It gives the teacher the broad direction for a topic or curriculum area.

  • Use it to: identify the overall learning focus before choosing activities.
  • When planning: read the CS together with the related Learning Standards, not in isolation.
  • Example (illustrative only): a broad focus on living things and their needs.
2

Learning Standard (LS)

The specific learning expectations.

What does LS make clear?

The Learning Standard specifies the learning expectation connected to a Content Standard. It helps the teacher identify what pupils should learn, demonstrate or communicate.

  • Use it to: write lesson objectives and choose suitable learning activities.
  • When planning: use the exact code and wording from the selected year’s official DSKP.
  • Assessment link: decide what observable evidence would show the intended learning.
3

Performance Standard (PS) & Performance Level (PL/TP)

Descriptors describe mastery; levels 1–6 indicate the reported performance level.

How do PS and PL/TP work together?

Performance Standard (PS) provides descriptors used to interpret the quality of pupils’ performance. Performance Level (PL, commonly labelled TP in the Malay DSKP) is the level from 1 to 6 that the teacher determines by referring to the relevant descriptor and evidence of learning.

  • TP1–TP6: represent an ordered range of performance levels. The exact meaning of each level depends on the descriptor for the relevant subject area and learning standard.
  • Use evidence: consider pupils’ responses, observations, practical work, explanations and other relevant evidence rather than assigning a level from one activity alone.
  • Use the DSKP: read the specific PS descriptors before making a judgement; do not assume one generic description applies to every topic.

Can this connect with Bloom’s Taxonomy?

Bloom’s Taxonomy can help a teacher vary the cognitive demand of questions and activities—for example, remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating and creating. It is a lesson-planning lens, not a direct conversion table for TP1–TP6. A Bloom verb alone does not determine a pupil’s performance level.

💡 Teacher reminder
Use CS to establish the broad focus, LS to clarify the intended learning, and PS descriptors with evidence to determine PL/TP. Bloom’s Taxonomy may support activity and question design, but never use it as a one-to-one substitute for official DSKP descriptors.
